item.title: US visa clash exposes Sudan’s forgotten war as foreign powers compete for strategic foothold
item.description: Abdel Fattah al-Burhan struck a defiant tone after Washington withheld his visa amid a dispute over a proposed 90-day humanitarian truce in Sudan.
item.content:encoded:
UNITED NATIONS — Sudan’s military leader is openly defying a U.S.-backed ceasefire push after Washington withheld his visa to attend the U.N. General Assembly, exposing a widening rift over a war that has become not only one of the world’s worst humanitarian disasters, but also a regional struggle for influence stretching to the Red Sea.

Gen. Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, head of Sudan’s armed forces and de facto leader, had been expected in New York during UNGA before the Trump administration withheld his visa amid a dispute over a proposed 90-day humanitarian truce. Days later, Burhan struck a defiant tone from Khartoum.

"We will keep our heads high. We will not accept bargaining, sell ourselves cheaply to anyone or bow to anyone," Burhan said Saturday, according to Anadolu Agency. "We do not need a visa to any country or anyone’s permission."

WORLD LEADERS DESCEND ON NEW YORK FOR UNGA — BUT WHO REALLY HAS AMERICA’S EAR?

The State Department has accused both Burhan’s Sudanese Armed Forces, or SAF, and the rival paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, or RSF, of failing to make serious commitments to an immediate truce.

"Neither the Sudanese Armed Forces, the Rapid Support Forces, nor their respective leaders, represent legitimate, constitutional governance for Sudan," State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott said Sept. 22, adding that the conduct of both leaders renders them "ineligible to govern the country."

The State Department said both sides had instead intensified combat operations and drone strikes that killed civilians and said Washington had repeatedly asked them to accept a humanitarian truce "without preconditions" and commit to an inclusive political dialogue leading to civilian government.

But a senior advisor to Burhan disputed Washington’s account in an on-camera interview with Fox News Digital on the sidelines of UNGA.

SUDAN'S FORGOTTEN WAR LEAVES MILLIONS HUNGRY AS GLOBAL ATTENTION REMAINS ELSEWHERE

Dr. Amjad Farid Al-Tayyib, the foreign affairs advisor to Sudan’s Transitional Sovereignty Council, said Sudan never rejected the American ceasefire proposal and instead submitted technical comments on it.

"We never rejected this proposal," Farid said. "The Sudanese government wants war with no one."

Farid said a negotiating team had intended to accompany Burhan and accused Washington of undermining the very diplomatic process it was seeking to advance by preventing the delegation from traveling.

The State Department declined to comment on Burhan’s specific visa case, citing its policy of not discussing individual visa decisions. A State Department spokesperson told Fox News Digital on background that Washington is instead focused on a broader diplomatic framework with Egypt, Saudi Arabia and the UAE through the Quad, linking a humanitarian truce and sustained aid access to a permanent ceasefire, civilian transition and reconstruction.

"We are working with our partners to encourage the parties to agree to the humanitarian truce and guarantee humanitarian access, and to also ensure external military or financial support to the warring parties is cut off," the spokesperson said.

The spokesperson added that the Quad supports the Quintet-led civilian political track and rejects parallel diplomatic processes that could fragment negotiations.

The United Nations also challenged Washington over the visa decision. "We immediately raised with the U.S. authorities the issue regarding the denial of visa to the President of the Transitional Sovereign Council of the Sudan, who was scheduled to address the General Assembly this week," U.N. Secretary-General spokesman Stéphane Dujarric told Fox News Digital.

PUTIN USING AFRICA AS ‘PURSE’ FOR UKRAINE WAR WHILE US FACES ‘INTELLIGENCE BLACK HOLE’: COMMANDER

Cameron Hudson, a former director for African affairs on the National Security Council who also served as chief of staff to successive U.S. presidential special envoys for Sudan, said his understanding was that Washington had asked the Sudanese to send a delegation both to the U.N. and to Washington for talks on a ceasefire.

He said the Sudanese were preparing to do so before Washington, in his understanding, made Burhan’s visa contingent on signing the ceasefire agreement before traveling.

"It doesn’t fully make sense why the United States took this decision at the last minute," Hudson told Fox News Digital.

Farid said the central dispute is whether the RSF would be required to withdraw from civilian areas it controls. He argued that freezing current lines of control risks turning a temporary ceasefire into a de facto partition of Sudan.

The dispute comes against the backdrop of a brutal civil war that erupted in April 2023 following a power struggle between Burhan and RSF commander Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, widely known as Hemedti.

Both sides have been accused of serious violations, but Hudson told Fox News Digital that treating their records as interchangeable obscures an important distinction.

"The RSF is committing war crimes on a scale and with an intention that the army does not," Hudson said.

Hudson said SAF has struck civilian targets and committed war crimes, including through drone attacks, but said the RSF’s record goes significantly further.

"They have committed mass rape, mass killing, torture, sexual enslavement," Hudson said, arguing that Western descriptions of "both sides" can create the impression that the two forces are committing the same crimes "on the same scale or with the same intention."

U.N. investigators have also drawn distinctions while documenting abuses by both forces.

AS WORLD FIXATES ON OTHER WARS, SUDAN SEES 12 MILLION FORCIBLY DISPLACED IN DEVASTATING CONFLICT

A U.N. fact-finding mission reported in September 2025 that both SAF and RSF were responsible for direct, large-scale attacks against civilians and the destruction of critical civilian infrastructure. But it found that the RSF, particularly during its siege of El Fasher and surrounding areas, committed crimes against humanity including murder, torture, enslavement, rape, sexual slavery, forced displacement and persecution on ethnic, gender and political grounds.

A separate U.N. Human Rights Office report released in February documented more than 6,000 killings during the first three days of the RSF’s final offensive on El Fasher and found that the violations could amount to war crimes and possible crimes against humanity.

Farid nevertheless accused the U.N. and Western governments of creating what he called a ‘false equivalence’ between Sudan’s military and the RSF.

"The U.N. is not staying neutral," he told Fox News Digital, arguing that international institutions have documented RSF atrocities without taking sufficient action against the group or those supporting it.

Farid nevertheless accused the U.N. and Western governments of creating what he called a false equivalence between Sudan’s military and the RSF.

U.N. Secretary-General spokesman Stéphane Dujarric rejected the allegation that the organization was equating the two sides. "This is not about equating two sides," Dujarric told Fox News Digital. "We focus on the facts, the violations that have been documented, and above all, the devastating toll this war has taken on civilians since 15 April 2023."

Dujarric said both the RSF and SAF have used explosive weapons in densely populated areas and that the U.N. Human Rights Office has documented attacks affecting schools, hospitals, markets and religious sites.

He pointed specifically to what he described as "particularly grave violations" by the RSF and affiliated forces in Darfur, including mass killings, sexual violence, torture, abductions and forced displacement, while noting that serious abuses have also been documented in SAF-controlled areas, including arbitrary detention, torture, ill-treatment and summary executions.

The war, meanwhile, increasingly extends beyond Sudan’s borders.

Foreign backing has become a central feature of the conflict. A July 2026 UK government assessment, drawing on U.N. and other reporting, said the RSF had benefited from support networks involving the UAE and neighboring countries, while SAF had received backing from states including Egypt, Iran, Pakistan and Turkey. The UAE has repeatedly denied providing military support to the RSF.

Fox News Digital reached out to the UAE Embassy in Washington and the UAE mission to the U.N. but did not receive a response in time for publication.

BAB EL-MANDEB STRAIT FACES GROWING THREAT AS HOUTHI ATTACKS RAISE FEARS OF A SECOND HORMUZ

Hudson said the RSF’s foreign relationships are only part of a much larger regional competition.

He said Egypt, Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Qatar have supported the army to varying degrees, while outside powers pursue their own strategic interests in Sudan.

That competition increasingly centers on Sudan’s Red Sea coastline. "There is a regional battle of influence among neighboring states and regional states who want to be able to control Sudan’s Red Sea coastline," Hudson said, pointing to potential military, port and economic access.

"Superimposed on top of the conflict inside Sudan is a regional proxy conflict for influence in Sudan and in the wider Horn of Africa, Red Sea region," he said.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio has also said foreign powers are central to prolonging the war. "What’s happening in Sudan would not be happening were it not for external actors supporting one side or the other," Rubio told reporters during UNGA week, describing U.S. efforts to secure even limited humanitarian agreements as "very frustrating."

Rubio said the parties have repeatedly agreed to commitments only to abandon them when one side believes it is gaining the upper hand. "There are external actors. I’m not going to single them out. You know who they are," Rubio said. "That war and that conflict and that crisis would not be happening were it not for the active participation of external actors that are feeding one side of that conflict or another."

He said meaningful progress would depend on those states pressuring their respective partners in Sudan.

"Until those external actors are prepared to use influence and pressure their respective proxies to live up to the commitments that they’re making, we’re not going to make progress," Rubio said.

WORLD'S HUMANITARIAN SYSTEM BUCKLING, 'NO LONGER FIT FOR PURPOSE,' US-BASED RESEARCHERS SAY

Sudan’s strategic value goes beyond geography. The country has significant gold, agricultural and livestock resources and sits at the crossroads of Africa and the Middle East. The World Bank has described Sudan as rich in fertile land, water and minerals, while noting its substantial gold production and agricultural potential.

Sudan also controls critical infrastructure used to transport South Sudanese crude oil to the Red Sea. A World Bank assessment says South Sudan’s oil has historically traveled through pipelines across Sudan to Port Sudan, its key export route.

Hudson said that broader regional competition helps explain why Washington has struggled to force Sudan’s outside backers to pull away.

"The United States is not going to use the limited political capital that it has with Saudi Arabia or Egypt or Turkey or UAE to get them to control their support to one side or the other in this conflict," he said.

Hudson also questioned Washington’s diplomatic strategy, arguing that pressure on Burhan has not been matched by sufficient direct engagement inside Sudan.

He said Massad Boulos, President Donald Trump’s senior advisor for Arab and African affairs, has never traveled to Sudan while attempting to mediate the conflict.

"He’s trying to mediate peace in a country that he’s never been to," Hudson said, arguing that Washington needs more "personal diplomacy" and less reliance on public statements and social media.

"If we want these people to sign a ceasefire deal, then they have to trust us," Hudson said. "And right now we’ve given them no reason to do so."

The U.N. acknowledged that international efforts have so far failed to stop the fighting. "Unfortunately, we are not seeing the war abating," Dujarric said, reiterating the U.N. position that "there is no military solution to the conflict," and noting Washington’s diplomatic role as the US and African Union co-chaired a Sept. 23 meeting bringing together the Quad and Quintet diplomatic groupings.

"The immediate priority is to stop the killing and secure a cessation of hostilities, while creating the conditions for a credible political process," he said.

item.title: Once again, no one knows when Josh Simmons will return — perhaps including the Chiefs
item.description: Josh Simmons has played just eight of 20 games since being drafted, and Andy Reid's vague updates on the Chiefs left tackle only deepen the mystery.
item.content:encoded:
Kansas City Chiefs left tackle Josh Simmons is mysteriously absent from the team — again.

Simmons holds one of the most important jobs in football. He is paid to protect the blindside of Patrick Mahomes, the central figure of the NFL’s defining dynasty and one of the most valuable assets in American sports.

Yet Simmons has played in just eight of 20 games since the Chiefs drafted him two seasons ago.

Khali Benson, an undrafted rookie right tackle who played exclusively on the right side in college, has filled in for Simmons this season. The Chiefs are 3-0, but Benson showed clear limitations on Sunday against the Dolphins. The team’s own highlights package of the victory is marred by defenders beating him almost immediately off the line of scrimmage.

The Chiefs offense misses Simmons' stability. And yet, there is still no information regarding when he might return, or whether he will return at all this season.

How does that happen in a league where highly paid insiders compete to deliver minute-by-minute injury updates on even the most obscure players in the NFL?

To understand how, we have to return to the 2025 pre-draft process.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

In October 2024, Simmons suffered a season-ending patellar tendon injury at Ohio State. After the season, reports indicated that he was well ahead of schedule in his recovery. The Chiefs selected him 32nd overall. A week after the draft, Simmons was active for rookie minicamp.

According to ESPN’s Jeremy Fowler, the national reporter most connected to the Chiefs, the injury did not cause Simmons to fall to the final pick of the first round. The concern was something less clinical and more ominous: his character.

"Several teams agree: Josh Simmons had best tape of any OT last year. And they aren't very concerned with recovery on the torn patella tendon. More of the concern is maturity/character. But he's going to the ideal, veteran-laden place," Fowler posted on X on April 24, 2025.

It remains unclear what those "character concerns" were. But they had to be substantial for nearly every team in the league to pass on a left tackle with elite tape who had already been cleared for contact by draft night.

For the first month of last season, it appeared the Chiefs had taken advantage of the rest of the league’s hesitation. Simmons looked like the long-term answer to Kansas City’s chronic left tackle problem.

That reading no longer holds.

On Oct. 6, 2025, two hours before the Chiefs’ Monday Night Football game against the Jacksonville Jaguars, the team abruptly listed Simmons as questionable due to an "illness." He ultimately played and played well.

The episode would have disappeared into the weekly churn of NFL oddities if not for what happened days later.

After a full week of practice, Simmons did not show up for his pregame responsibilities the following Sunday against the Lions. It was reported that players and members of the staff were unsure of his whereabouts. After the game, head coach Andy Reid suggested he knew where Simmons was.

Reid and the Chiefs offered almost no explanation afterward. The silence continued throughout much of Simmons’ four-game absence, which the team described only as a personal/family issue.

Reporters provided no real clarity over the past year about what happened or why members of the organization were apparently unaware of Simmons’ absence until close to game time.

Last month, Sports Illustrated’s Matt Verderame provided the first substantive report on the matter, saying Simmons left the team without approval the Saturday before the Lions game and that there was a period of time in which the "team didn't know where he was."

That is also the version of the story OutKick has heard but have been unable to independantly verify. The team will not confirm, deny, or comment on the matter. OutKick emailed Chiefs general manager Brett Veach and Simmons’ agent Drew Rosenhaus before Verderame’s report to ask whether those details were accurate. Neither responded.

Which brings us back to the present.

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON’T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

After a full training camp, Simmons missed his first practice of the season on Aug. 18. Verderame reported afterward that Simmons was "fine."

"On Chiefs LT Josh Simmons missing practice with a back injury, I’m told 'he’s fine.' Don’t sense any concern about the second-year star," Verderame posted on X.

It is now Sept. 28. Simmons has not practiced since. He has missed the first three games of the season. Though the team says he has been in the building, he's clearly not "fine."

However, we have already established that Verdemran's sources with the team are strong. There is reason to believe that the team did consider Simmons' injury minor at the time.

Something changed.

On Monday, Reid offered a vague, almost eerie update.

"I’ll tell you what," Reid told Chiefs Digest reporter Matt Derrick. "I will let you guys know when Josh [Simmons] is coming back. I’ll be the first to tell you. So we’ll just see how that all works out."

The contrast with Reid’s other injury updates is difficult to ignore. Asked about safety Chamarris Connor, who, like Simmons, is the only other starter to miss the team’s first three games, Reid sounded far more direct.

"Yeah, so he practiced last week, and he’ll get going this week, too," Reid said. "So there’s a good chance he’ll be out there. We’ll just see how the week goes, but it looks like it’ll be a pretty decent chance."

Now consider the reporting around other injured Chiefs players. When rookie Mansoor Delane injured his shoulder in Week 1, Adam Schefter, Ian Rapoport, and Tom Pelissero quickly reported that the injury was minor and continued providing updates throughout the week.

ESPN, Fox, NFL Network, NBC and Amazon devote weekly pregame segments to injury news. They inform viewers about the availability of backup linebackers and rotational defensive backs. Yet we cannot find a single example of them discussing the status of the player tasked with protecting Patrick Mahomes.

Over the past month, there has been one national report about Simmons. It came from Fowler, who, fittingly, described the injury as "mysterious."

We keep coming back to that word.

At minimum, we can establish this: the NFL’s top reporters either do not know the story behind Simmons’ absence or are choosing not to pursue it publicly.

Likewise, the Chiefs either do not know when Simmons will return or are deliberately withholding information they routinely provide about other players.

That is unusual, to use a term.

Simmons’ absence has naturally invited speculation about whether it is connected to last year’s disappearance from the team.

Yahoo NFL analyst Hayden Winks is among those asking.

"So Josh Simmons is going to miss more time than what he would've on IR, which could mean he's missing longer than the Chiefs expected based on this back injury. There's also a history of him just not being around. There could be a lot more to this story than what's public," he posted Monday.

Price Carter is one of the top Chiefs film analysts. He detailed the unusualness of the Simmons saga to OutKick:

"It would be difficult to describe the Josh Simmons injury timeline as normal. What started out as a routine back injury, described by several reporters as a 'minor issue' that he could 'play if it was game week' has now lingered on for the better part of two months. With no timeline for return, and no corresponding roster move the local media is only left with the information they are given by the team. Andy Reid is notorious for not saying much at the podium and the team only provides a very brief look at practice to the media. Reporters state that Simmons is with the team but that is all the news that there is."

That speculation is warranted. Simmons is not an anonymous private employee. He is the left tackle for the Kansas City Chiefs. And by offering so little clarity, his own team has invited the public to fill in the blanks.

Perhaps there is a deeper explanation for Simmons’ absence. Maybe the pre-draft character concerns are connected to last year’s absence and this year’s. There is precedent for NFL teams describing a personal matter as an injury in an effort to protect a player. The Bills did this with Ed Oliver in the face of tragedy.

Still, the Chiefs have made the matter worse by saying nothing while keeping Simmons on the active roster. They could have placed him on injured reserve and said they would re-evaluate him later in the season. They could have placed him on the non-football injury list and said he was out until further notice while asking the public to respect his privacy.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Instead, the Chiefs have chosen ambiguity.

The longer this lingers without an explanation, the harder it becomes to accept that this is merely a back injury. If it were only a back injury, why the secrecy? Why the lack of reporting? Why the careful language?

For whatever reason, the Kansas City Chiefs do not want to provide the details about Josh Simmons.

Already, there is speculation that Simmons does not want to play or does not love football. At this juncture, how can that not be among the possibilities that come to mind?

At this point, Kansas City owes Simmons and its fans one of two things: an explanation, or a roster decision that acknowledges there is no clear path back.

Apparently, the team has concluded that rampant speculation about its stud left tackle is less damaging than the truth.

item.title: Phillies manager Don Mattingly delivers expletive-laden speech as team makes playoffs after Game 162 win
item.description: Don Mattingly's expletive-filled locker room speech fired up the Philadelphia Phillies after clinching the final NL Wild Card spot in Game 162.
item.content:encoded:
It doesn’t matter how you make it into the MLB playoffs – it’s what you do when you get there.

That was basically the message Philadelphia Phillies manager Don Mattingly had for his team on Sunday after winning Game 162 to avoid a massive collapse for a team many pegged to be a potential World Series candidate out of the National League.

Mattingly just added some not-safe-for-work verbiage in there.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

The Phillies, with a 7-3 win over the Tampa Bay Rays, secured the final NL Wild Card slot with an 88-74 record out of the NL East.

Before champagne was popped in the locker room after their win on Sunday night, Mattingly, who was named interim manager after Rob Thomson was fired early in the 2026 MLB season, made sure to let his players know how he felt about heading into the postseason.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

"F--- that, it doesn’t matter how you get in, you just got to get in. And we’re f---ing in," he said before everyone joined in the celebration.

Philadelphia began the season 9-19, shocking much of the baseball world considering how great their roster is. It led to Thomson’s firing, and Mattingly was tasked with getting the team back on track.

Much like the situation with the Boston Red Sox and the Alex Cora firing, the Phillies saw a resurgence with new leadership in the dugout. However, the Phillies got back to their slumping ways at the worst possible time.

Through the final weeks of the season, the Phillies were fighting tooth and nail to secure one of the NL Wild Card positions alongside other postseason hopefuls. Then, by the time Sunday rolled around for the final game of the regular season, The Phillies had lost six of their last eight games with the Arizona Diamondbacks doing the exact opposite to challenge the right to play for a title.

Just last week, the Phillies held a four-game lead over the D-backs for the last Wild Card spot, but they were forced into a win-or-go-home situation on Sunday night against the AL East-winning Tampa Bay Rays – owners of the best record in the American League.

The Phillies got the job done, but they ultimately didn’t have to after the San Diego Padres defeated the Diamondbacks, 9-4, in their final game of the year.

While the Phillies are in, their plans for the Wild Card Series changes considering Zack Wheeler, their presumptive Game 1 starter, had to pitch on Sunday to keep their season alive.

Mattingly and Phillies will now face a familiar foe, as the NL East-winning Atlanta Braves will host them for the best-of-three series starting Tuesday.

item.title: DHS sends ominous warning as migrant caravan heads toward US-Mexico border from Honduras
item.description: A Honduran migrant caravan numbered in the hundreds has crossed into Mexico and is moving north as DHS warns the days of catch and release are over.
item.content:encoded:
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) issued a strong warning to a major migrant caravan that crossed into Mexico and was moving north with hopes of reaching the U.S.-Mexico border.

"USBP is closely engaged with its international partners to monitor their movement and any additional developments," DHS told Fox News in a statement. "[United States Border Patrol] USBP reminds migrants that under the leadership of President Trump and Homeland Secretary Mullin, the border has remained closed and secured for the last 16 months."

The caravan, numbering in the hundreds as of Monday, is predominantly made up of Hondurans, Guatemalans, Salvadorans, Ecuadoreans and Haitians.

The USBP said the caravan departed San Pedro Sula, Honduras on Sept. 20.

TRUMP ADMIN MARKS 15 STRAIGHT MONTHS WITH ZERO BORDER RELEASES AS APPREHENSIONS PLUNGE 94%

Any migrants considering making the journey to the southern border should be aware that the days of "catch and release" are over, "and Biden’s disastrous open border policy has been SEALED SHUT," DHS said.

TRUMP REAFFIRMS ICE ARREST POLICY AFTER CONFUSING GUIDANCE SPARKS ALARM AMONG AGENTS

"Anyone attempting to illegally enter the United States will be apprehended, prosecuted, and removed from the country," DHS said.

Reports of the caravan came amid a contentious midterm election cycle where the Trump administration's crackdown on illegal immigration has been a popular talking point from both sides of the political aisle.

FEDERAL APPEALS COURT DEALS BLOW TO TRUMP DEPORTATION AGENDA

President Donald Trump has mandated sweeping deportations and expanded crackdowns nationwide amid historically low levels of illegal immigration since he took office last year.

Some migrants said they were headed to the U.S. for better economic opportunities.

"I want to reach the United States," Honduran migrant José Zelaya, traveling with seven relatives, told the Spanish-language EFE news agency, the Houston Chronicle reported.

He said the caravan had no organized leadership, adding that "hunger and need" were the driving forces behind the journey.

item.title: 'Insulting': Ex-Trump official's 'dishonest' campaign ad triggers conservative revolt
item.description: GOP Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders' reelection ad depicting a white-male welfare recipient named "Brad" drew conservative backlash online.
item.content:encoded:
Republican Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders ignited backlash from conservatives Monday after releasing a campaign ad depicting a young White man as the face of welfare abuse, with critics arguing the portrayal was misleading.

The ad, released as Huckabee Sanders runs for reelection on new welfare work requirements, follows a fictional character named "Brad," who is portrayed as an able-bodied White man spending his days playing video games, lounging on the couch and avoiding work while relying on taxpayer-funded benefits. Huckabee Sanders argues her proposal would require able-bodied adults without dependents to work, train for a job or volunteer in order to continue receiving assistance.

"Meet Brad," Huckabee Sanders starts the ad. "Brad has turned relaxing into a full-time profession. But you – you actually work hard. You pay taxes to cover welfare for guys like Brad who just choose not to work."

Huckabee Sanders faced backlash from conservatives who slammed the campaign's execution, arguing the decision to depict a young White man as the face of welfare abuse did not reflect reality.

FLORIDA BECOMES FIRST STATE TO BLOCK WELFARE CASH FOR TATTOOS, VAPES AND MORE

"Great policy," Co-founder and CEO of The Federalist Sean Davis argued. "Terrible ad that is so dishonest and insulting that it will entirely overshadow the genuinely great policy."

"This is a massive own goal, [Sarah Huckabee Sanders], and you should fire the consultants who made this ad," Will Chamberlain, the Article III Project senior counsel, posted on X. "Do not portray your core voting bloc as losers, period. "

"White males are the Republican Party's voting base and yet they are the group the Republican Party sh—s on at every possible opportunity," responded Daily Wire's Matt Walsh. "Meanwhile, back in reality, women are significantly more likely to be on welfare than men. And black people are astronomically more likely to be on welfare than white people. So the number of single young white male 'Brads' abusing the welfare system is minuscule."

WARNOCK WARNS DEMS TO CUT THE 'JARGON' AND SPEAK 'PLAIN ENGLISH' WITH YOUNG MEN WHO FEEL LEFT BEHIND

"Attacking white (specifically Christian) young men is the most acceptable political tactic in America thanks to the evils of liberalism," said the American Principles Project's Caleb Pascoe. "It's staggering how much even the majority of GOP politicians feel safe attacking white young men, instead of communicating the truth of welfare, because they might get called 'racist' or whatever."

"Always a white male villain in these ads," another conservative account wrote. "I hate the GOP so much it’s unreal."

After the initial post got millions of views, Huckabee Sanders followed up with an X post that said, "Some critics online don't like my welfare work requirement ad. Next thing you know they’ll say I should have used cookies instead of cheese balls."

"If you are able-bodied you should not collect welfare simply because you choose not to work. Period. WATCH->" she continued, which invited conservatives to attack the video again.

"Your ad targeted and mocked the one demographic—young white men—that is least likely to be on welfare and yet the most likely to be illegally locked out of the job market," Davis added in a follow-up post. "Why?"

"Is this an op?" another account wrote.

EX-HOUSE FREEDOM CAUCUS CHAIR SAYS GOP ISN'T 'A CONSERVATIVE PARTY ANYMORE,' BUT DEMOCRATS ARE 'WORSE'

The unusual backlash from the right also attracted attention from critics on the left, who seized on the intra-conservative dispute over the ad.

Among them was left-wing commentator Keith Olbermann, who mocked what he called the "White Power GOP Party" for turning on Huckabee Sanders over the ad's depiction of a white welfare recipient.

"Huck puts out the first honest TV ad by a republican in 75 years and the White Power GOP Party is big mad that the welfare leech shown is a white guy named Brad," Olbermann said amid the backlash.

"Republicans are insanely mad this Sarah Huckabee Sanders ad portrays a white gamer guy as the face of welfare," Will Sommer, a senior reporter for The Bulwark, posted on X.

"Republicans in the comments are furious that Sarah Huckabee Sanders dared to depict a white man on welfare and are blaming "jews," far-left media company MeidasTouch posted on X. "The Republican Party has a massive racism and antisemitism problem."

Fox News Digital reached out to Huckabee Sanders' team for comment but did not hear back in time for publication.

item.title: Comedian Matt Rife says he ditched Hollywood's old playbook for success after hitting 'rock bottom'
item.description: Matt Rife reveals he "hated" TikTok but the platform's viral reach gave him what years of chasing Hollywood's traditional comedy pipeline never could.
item.content:encoded:
Matt Rife said Monday on "Fox & Friends" that social media has fundamentally changed how comedians break into the entertainment industry, explaining that posting viral crowd work clips on TikTok accomplished what years of chasing Hollywood's traditional stand-up pipeline could not.

Inside the Walmart Arkansas Music Pavilion ahead of his show, Rife told Fox News that when he moved from his hometown in Ohio to Los Angeles, he expected to follow the long-established path of becoming a regular at famous comedy clubs in hopes of landing television appearances and sitcom roles. 

Instead, after early success on MTV's "Wild 'N Out" faded, he found himself back at professional "rock bottom" before social media unexpectedly transformed his career.

DAVID CROSS DOESN’T 'GIVE A F---’: THE ACTOR-COMEDIAN ON HIS NEW SPECIAL, SOCIAL MEDIA AND ‘TERRIFYING’ AI

"That's why I moved to LA, was to maybe become a regular at, like, the Laugh Factory, Comedy Store or the Improv, where these talent scouts would come out and they'd find you. You'd do a late-night set and then maybe you'd get a small part on a sitcom. Maybe you get your own show based on your material. That's what I was striving for," he said.

Rife previously told Dave Portnoy during a podcast appearance that he was averaging between $40-60 thousand a year in Los Angeles before finding social media fame. According to the Los Angeles County Development Authority, Rife's prior annual salary meant he was dubbed "very low income" by the city's cost of living standards at the time.

Then, Rife discovered TikTok, and the rest is history.

With a current reported net worth of $40-50 million, the comedian emphasized that he "hated" TikTok and "never wanted to be a part of it" — but that didn't stop him from accruing the 20.3 million followers he has today on that platform alone.

JAY LENO CALLS JOE ROGAN 'THE NEW JOHNNY CARSON' AS HE REFLECTS ON WHAT CHANGED IN LATE-NIGHT TELEVISION

"It's insane. The reach on there is incomparable," he told Fox News.

item.title: Lane Kiffin is already somehow blaming the SEC's new conference schedule for LSU's injuries
item.description: Lane Kiffin is already blaming LSU's injuries on the SEC's new nine-game conference schedule, despite the Tigers having played just two league games.
item.content:encoded:
For years, the SEC has enjoyed a bit of an advantage over other conferences when it comes to record, rankings, and strength of schedule: they played fewer conference games.

The Pac-12, when that conference existed in its previous form, for example, played nine games against other conference teams. So did the Big Ten. The SEC, however, had just eight. With four non-conference opponents, some schools could choose to schedule four likely wins, before entering SEC play.

An ideal example is the 2025 Missouri Tigers. Missouri's non-conference slate was Central Arkansas, Kansas, Louisiana, and Massachusetts. Four games in which they'd be overwhelming favorites, four wins secured before conference play started.

FLORIDA GATORS, MISSISSIPPI STATE SOAR, USC TUMBLES IN LATEST INEXPLICABLE AP TOP 25 POLL

Missouri proceeded to win just four conference games, 29-20 over South Carolina, 23-17 over Auburn in double overtime, a 49-27 win over Mississippi State, and 31-17 over Arkansas. But, thanks in large part to their four scheduled wins, the Tigers remained in the AP Poll for most of the season, providing a "ranked" opponent for Texas A&M, Vanderbilt, Alabama, and Oklahoma. They did not beat a team that finished the season with a winning record on their way to finishing 8-4.

Incredibly, with this resume, the Tigers were ranked in 12 of 16 polls during the regular season. And why not? 8-4 doesn't look bad, does it? That's a solid season in a tough conference, if you aren't paying close attention. Now remove one of those scheduled non-conference wins, and suddenly the road to 8-4 looks a lot harder. Which is the point other conferences made when arguing against the SEC's endless complaints about strength of schedule.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Well, for 2026, the SEC finally moved to nine conference games and eliminated the "extra" win many of the member programs used to their advantage. And even through just a few weeks of conference play, new LSU Tigers head coach Lane Kiffin is already using it as an excuse.

Ahead of last weekend's matchup against Texas A&M, Kiffin complained sarcastically, and inaccurately, about the perceived scheduling issues hurting the Tigers with Marcel

"Obviously we just played the best one in the country last week thinking he can hurt you even when you have the right call on and everybody covered and a guy comes free," he said. "Obviously he (Chambliss) played great a year ago here in the stadium, so this is one of those scheduling quirks just like last week where never in that LSU-Ole Miss series had it ever been played two times in a row."

That was, of course, incorrect, but Kiffin wasn't done there in going after the SEC for its scheduling practices. LSU is dealing with its fair share of injuries through the first few weeks of the season, including to star linebacker Whit Wheeks and tight end Trey'Dez Green.

Per ESPN's Marty Smith, LSU's injuries are a direct result of the SEC's nine-game conference schedule. Which is odd because his team has played just two conference games so far.

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

Smith posted that Kiffin explained that it's an indication of the differences "versus other conferences, and how (they) don’t have to play players or play them as long."

"Be careful what you wish for, SEC," Kiffin said.

Ah. Yes. Classic Lane Kiffin. There is no outcome that doesn't have a predetermined excuse. No other schools face injuries. No other games require playing starters. When the SEC had eight conference games, it wasn't an advantage, but with nine, they're at a significant disadvantage. Even when they've only played two conference games so far. One of those games was against a very bad Texas A&M team, where the score was 35-6 in the fourth quarter and the outcome was never in much doubt.

The Tigers shouldn't have much to worry about with powerhouse McNeese State coming into town next weekend either.

Curiously, Kiffin never addresses the impact of travel, rest, and recovery on other conferences. Like, for example, USC, which played a road game in New Jersey, then turned around and played a home game in LA a week later. That's a ~6,000 mile round trip road game. LSU's longest road trip of the season is Lexington, Kentucky. Their entire travel schedule is less than one USC road game. That stuff matters as Kiffin would say if it were impacting his team.

UCLA has road games traveling 8,120 one-way miles. USC is 9,500 miles. Just a few examples. The "woe is me" act Kiffin puts on might be effective for the SEC boosters in friendly media outlets. It's just not backed up by any reality we live in. But it's a near-certainty he'll be running the same playbook after the season to try and get the SEC back to eight conference games. Then he'll find something else to complain about.

item.title: DR. MARC SIEGEL: What 18 years at Fox taught me about courage and faith
item.description: Benjamin Hall recalls the Ukraine war attack that killed his crew and the miraculous Ukrainian special forces rescue that he believes was a sign from God.
item.content:encoded:
I joined Fox in early 2008 as a contributor. I was struck from the beginning by the network's flexibility and creativity, allowing me to expand my role from expertise in infectious diseases to health policy and Obamacare.

I was able to flex various journalistic muscles, too. I was sent to Phoenix to examine Sen. John McCain’s health records but ended up with the opportunity to deliver on-air reports.

I began to report for the network in earnest in 2012, and then in the spring of 2013, during the Boston Marathon, when two self-radicalized brothers executed the largest terrorist attack on U.S. soil since 9/11, I managed to get permission from our top executives to head up there.

DR MARC SIEGEL: TWENTY-FIVE YEARS AFTER 9/11, THE DEADLY HEALTH CRISIS IS STILL CLAIMING LIVES

On the way, I somehow convinced the PR team at Massachusetts General Hospital (MGH) to grant me the very first interview with a survivor — a woman. Our excellent production team wasn’t expecting me, as we had our top reporters already in the field, but they quickly transitioned to supporting and guiding me. She had been blown off her feet and badly wounded her leg. Her would-be boyfriend had carried her down one-way streets (going in the opposite direction of the cars) to MGH.

We were ready. She looked straight into the camera and said, "We can’t let the terrorists win. We must stay strong and not be afraid. Boston is a great city."

Ten years later, another top Fox executive sent me to East Palestine, Ohio, following the train wreck there. One of the best field producers in the business came with me, and while I was in the neighborhood doughnut shop sampling the best doughnuts I’d ever had, she was assembling an array of guests who had all been injured or affected by the toxic smoke.

FOX NEWS MEDIA'S SPOTLIGHT AWARDS CELEBRATE BEHIND-THE-SCENES STARS AS NETWORK NEARS 30 YEARS

The ERs in the area were calling it "situational anxiety," but outside the temporary state health facility, I interviewed patients who were having trouble breathing while the smoke in the air gave everyone, myself included, a sore throat. People who swam in the river developed rashes, and the long-term health risks remained unknown.

The angels of Fox are the executives, producers, and bookers who have the vision and work ethic to seek out and present stories that would otherwise be missed.

We are a family that has developed strong bonds, and we look out for each other. When my father died earlier this year at age 102, the entire Fox management team, from the CEO on down, came to the funeral.

BENJAMIN HALL TACKLES GRUELING ONE WORLD TRADE CENTER CLIMB ON PROSTHETIC LEGS TO HONOR FALLEN HEROES

Senior Correspondent Ben Hall brings out the best in the Fox team, and they inspire him. Chief National Security Correspondent Jennifer Griffin was crucial to arranging his extraction from Ukraine after a horrific near-death experience when his car was bombed and his cameraman and producer were killed in 2022. He survived, thanks to many angels, messengers from God, as I write in my new book, "THE ANGELS AMONG US."

Here’s what Benjamin Hall shared with me about what he was thinking on the day he and his team were attacked in Ukraine:

"At this moment of trying to stay strong, I think of how I am going to get home. I think of my children. Our car has burned totally to pieces, and we are down on the road, down a slight little dip in the road where we are lying, and this one car comes out of nowhere, and it drives past us. And I am shouting at it, ‘We’re here! We’re here!’ And it doesn’t see us, and it keeps driving. And it is a car of Ukrainian special forces, and this same car, amazingly, has engine trouble ten minutes or so down the road, and they have to stop to figure that out. And because of that, they drive back again!"

Hall believes this event is a sign directly from God.

DANA PERINO: THE UNTOLD STORY OF THE REMARKABLE PEOPLE WHO MAKE FOX NEWS POSSIBLE

"I have pulled myself further up by this time, dragging myself along, up toward the road, and as the car comes back again, I don’t know it’s coming. There it is… The last thing I remember is this guy jumping out. He grabs my body armor, grabs the back of my arm, and pulls me along the ground, running to his car."

Is the vision of his daughter that he sees after the missile hits actually an angel? It’s the question everyone has, and I ask it of Hall.

MARTHA MACCALLUM: AFTER 22 YEARS, HERE'S WHY I'M GRATEFUL TO CALL FOX HOME

"Yeah, 100%, either she is an angel that comes to me when I need her, and she gives me the strength I need, and she brings me back, or it is because my body and my mind are calling for her. It’s after the first and then the second shell, when I go into this other world, that’s when I get shrapnel in the eye, and it takes out part of my skull. So, I am already pretty badly injured at this point. Then the third shell takes off my leg, my foot. But I’ve no doubt that my daughter is sent to me, and either it is God who sends her or my body needs it, and my mind goes to the place it has to go to find the right strength."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

Ben Hall’s father had recently died in 2022, and Hall had just buried him when he flew from his father’s funeral straight to Ukraine. Hall can feel his father is there with him as well. It’s as if his father’s life has joined with his own now that his spirit has moved on to the next world, into heaven. His father gives him strength. His daughter is there with him, and so is his father.

Fox News loves Ben Hall, and his courage and strength inspire all of us.

item.title: 'Lioness' star Zoe Saldaña says she can't imagine taking on another Taylor Sheridan role

item.title: 'Nobody Wants This' star accuses Israel of 'genocide'
item.description: Actor Adam Brody called the Israel-Hamas conflict "genocide" while discussing his growing political activism on behalf of a progressive organization.
item.content:encoded:
On Friday, Jewish actor Adam Brody joined the growing list of progressive celebrities accusing Israel of committing "genocide" in Gaza while suggesting that Hollywood has grown more "conservative" under President Donald Trump.

Brody, who plays a rabbi in Netflix’s romantic comedy series "Nobody Wants This," addressed the topic when speaking to GQ Magazine about his political activism and volunteer work for the progressive organization Swing Left. Although he has not publicly addressed the Middle East conflict previously, Brody told the magazine that he has discussed it privately.

"Put me down as thinking it's a genocide," Brody said. "Put me down as wanting a free Palestine. It's awful that it's taken so much death and misery, but it does feel like it's reaching a breaking point that it should have a while ago. I'm hopeful that another administration can really do some good and correct some of these policies that are helping that situation be as awful as it is."

FORMULA ONE DRIVER LEWIS HAMILTON TELLS MACKLEMORE HE IS ‘STANDING’ IN SOLIDARITY WITH HIM ON PALESTINE

"The O.C." actor's comments resembled ones made by other progressive celebrities such as actor Mark Ruffalo and rapper Macklemore, who have referred to the Israel-Hamas conflict as a "genocide."

Though several celebrities have spoken out against Israel's actions, Brody suggested that political activism in Hollywood has decreased, noting that he doesn't speak about political issues in many interviews.

"I think it's the cycle. The first time Trump was elected, it was inconceivable. It woke everyone," he said. "There was so much activism. People were running for office that had never ran before. It was so awful to watch him defile our government, our country, our reputation, and really pit people against each other. I felt like most of the country right away was really against it."

"It felt very safe to step out against him in the first presidency," Brody continued. "The second time, the presidency was more powerful. Corporations were lining up behind him like they hadn't before. People had to risk more to get in front of it. It just felt like the mood wasn't there. The country decided this is the way it wants to go. As we start to pick up steam for this election, it's getting exciting again. We're starting to feel powerful again."

'SHE-HULK' STAR SLAMS TOM SELLECK, MICHAEL JORDAN AS 'COWARDLY' FOR AVOIDING POLITICAL TALK

Brody even claimed that Hollywood has gotten more "outspokenly" conservative during Trump's second term.

"Again, as one side has more power, it makes sense that it draws people to it for all the human reasons that would be attractive: groupthink, your own well-being, your own money and success," Brody said.

Fox News Digital reached out to Brody's representatives for comment but did not immediately receive a response. 

In response to the interview, "Hollywood in Toto" founder Christian Toto told Fox News Digital that while it has gotten "microscopically better" to be a conservative in Hollywood, groupthink and bullying behind the scenes "remain powerful" as activism starts to see a resurgence.

MICHAEL RAPAPORT TELLS CRAIG CARTON THAT HIS SUPPORT FOR ISRAEL HAS COST HIM WORK IN HOLLYWOOD

"Hollywood activism was a bit muted following the 2024 election, but now it's back to its usual volume and cadence. And if Brody truly felt afraid to say what he's saying ... he would keep it all to himself. Sharing his doctrinaire, hard-Left views is the most pro-career move an actor can make in 2026, particularly in how he's viewed by fellow actors," Toto said.

item.title: El-Sayed questions ethics of football in resurfaced audio

item.content:encoded:
Michigan U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed took aim at football culture, questioning whether America's most popular sport is "ethical," according to a resurfaced audio clip posted online Monday by the Republican Party.

item.title: Cam Ward's sister says her family has been target of 'threats, harassment' by fans angry about brother's play
item.description: Chantel Ward says she and her family face threats, harassment, and bullying after Cam Ward's struggles as the Tennessee Titans' starting quarterback.
item.content:encoded:
The price of celebrity and a big-dollar NFL contract for Tennessee Titans starting quarterback Cam Ward is apparently being paid, in part, by his family. They have been the target of "threats, harassment, and bullying," according to his sister.

Chantel Ward says she is one of the targets because her brother is obviously not playing up to the expectations of being the team's 2025 first-round Draft pick.

She laid bare her feelings on the issue on Monday — not coincidentally after Ward struggled in the winless Titans' 12-7 loss at home to the New York Giants.

"The fact I even have to post this is diabolical," Ward, the player's 27-year-old older sister, posted on her Instagram account.

IS CYBERBULLYING HIDING IN YOUR CHILD'S GROUP CHAT?

"People see the football games. They see the wins, the losses, the interceptions, the touchdowns, the press conferences and everything that happens on the field. What they don't see is what comes with it for the people who love these players when the game is over."

What typically happens is the families of well-paid players who were drafted first overall, as Ward was, live a privileged life.

But there's more, according to Chantel Ward. Because that life has its obstacles and major concerns.

And getting online threats has apparently become one of those for the Wards.

WILL LEVIS SUPREMELY CONFIDENT HE IS CAPABLE OF BEING NFL STARTER WHILE BATTLING FOR TITANS' BACKUP ROLE

"After games, people come directly to my DMs on Facebook, Twitter, and Instagram with threats, hate, bullying, personal attacks, and disrespect toward me and my family – all over football," she wrote.

Ward made the point that it is fair to be critical of players because that's part of the sport. Play good, all good.

Play badly, there is fallout.

Everyone understands that.

"Criticize the game," Ward wrote. "Criticize a play. Be frustrated with your team. That's sports, and I completely understand that. But seeking out a player's sister, parents, or other family members to personally attack them because you're upset about what happened on a football field is something completely different.

"Cam is a quarterback to y'all. He's entertainment on Sundays. To me, that's my little brother. Somebody I've loved, protected, supported, and watched work for his entire life.

SOME TITANS PLAYERS ARRIVE AT THEIR GAME SUNDAY AGAINST THE EAGLES LOOKING RIDICULOUS

"So when people come to my page or into my messages is disrespecting him, me or my family, and then tell me, 'Don't take it personal' – how exactly am I supposed to take it?

"And trust me, the screenshots I share are only a fraction of what comes through. There's so much that happens outside of those football games that people will never see."

Ward shared a screenshot on her story of someone who answered and said her brother "shouldn't play like a f——-g r — —d and people would come in here and congratulate you."

Ward did not share a post proving the family has received threats, but she made the allegation that she's flooded by them.

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

"Criticize football all you want," she wrote. "Criticize performance. Criticize the decisions. That comes with the territory.

"But threats, harassment, bullying, and attacking someone's family will never be just part of the game."

One more thing: If the Wards are indeed enduring threats online and are afraid those might manifest where they live, they should contact authorities.

At minimum, the quarterback should alert the Titans.

PLYMOUTH, Mass. — Lindsay Clancy's legal team and Massachusetts prosecutors have agreed to delay defense attorney Kevin Reddington’s motion to investigate the lone holdout juror in her mistrial, his attorney Edward Paltzik told Fox News' Kayleigh McEnany Monday.

"The DA and Reddington consent to adjourn the motion to investigate Michael," Paltzik said. "If Judge Sullivan signs an order today, much of it could be adjourned. Either way, a status conference is still likely. But the motion about Michael is likely not on tomorrow."

Clancy attorney Kevin Reddington, however, fired back a short time later in a fiery statement of his own, calling Paltzik's statement "pure nonsense" while conceding that he and county prosecutors had agreed to a continuation as a "professional courtesy" to local counsel now working with the holdout juror.

A final decision is subject to Judge William Sullivan, but the judge has not yet announced a decision one way or the other. The delay agreement comes as the juror's new local counsel informed the parties that he does not have access to impounded information necessary to prepare a response.

LINDSAY CLANCY ATTORNEY KEVIN REDDINGTON FIRES BACK AT LONE HOLDOUT JUROR'S ATTORNEY AFTER FIERY INTERVIEW

"Earlier today, both the government and I were contacted by a professional local attorney who represents Juror Doe," Reddington said, not naming Desronvil due to an impoundment order from the court. "That attorney requested — as any qualified counsel would — adequate time to review our motion and reply. As is professional courtesy, both the government and I agreed to continue this specific motion to a later date at their request."

He said the motion "remains active, fully alive, and is currently pending a ruling."

"We will not allow a publicity-seeking opportunist to twist simple courtroom courtesy into a victory that does not exist," he added. 

Clancy is due in court at 9 a.m. Tuesday for a status conference in the wake of her mistrial — her first court date since jurors deadlocked on Sept. 4.

"We have our local counsel showing up either way," Paltzik said. "It’s important to note that all of this is subject to the Judge’s discretion."

The hearing was expected to cover Reddington's motion to hold an inquiry into the holdout, Michael Desronvil, as well as a double jeopardy motion seeking to dismiss the charges instead of holding a retrial.

Prosecutors are also expected to give an update on their plans.

Reddington had asked the court for an investigation into Desronvil, the only juror out of 12 who maintained that Clancy is guilty of murder in the strangling deaths of her three children, Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months.

Eleven other jurors agreed that Clancy should be found not guilty by reason of mental defect or disease after Reddington raised an insanity defense, arguing that she suffered from postpartum psychosis.

Paltzik also questioned why Reddington didn't object to his client as a potential juror during jury selection.

"I just learned that Kevin ‘Shooter McGavin’ Reddington HAD multiple peremptory challenges remaining when the opportunity to strike Michael came around," he wrote on X Monday, in a reference to a character from the movie "Happy Gilmore." 

"Reddington could have eliminated Michael during jury selection but failed to do so," he wrote.

item.title: Comedian Nate Bargatze reveals biggest failing as car owner in unlikely new role
item.description: Known for his family-friendly comedy, Nate Bargatze has teamed up with the Ford Motor Company on a new car business campaign. Fox News Digital spoke with him about his humor.
item.content:encoded:
FIRST ON FOX — Comedian Nate Bargatze, the Tennessee native and dad who has made a name for himself with his clean-cut, family-friendly comedy, is stressing relatability, simplicity and trust as he moves into a new realm. 

He's the average guy who doesn't know it all — and freely admits he needs help. 

Bargatze says in a new ad, "Look, I don’t know how to take care of my truck. But the technicians at Ford Service — they do."

NATE BARGATZE REVEALS FAMILY-FOCUSED VISION BEHIND $350M NASHVILLE THEME PARK AHEAD OF HIS FIRST MOVIE RELEASE 

The Ford Motor Company on Monday announced Bargatze as the face of a new "Real Parts. Real Pros. Real Easy" customer service campaign.

"I haven't really done a lot of stuff like this," the comedian told Fox News Digital in a recent on-camera interview.

He said that when Ford asked him about being involved, "I was super excited. I'm a big Ford [fan]. I have a Ford Bronco. I love Ford — it's an iconic company. They've been around for a long time."

He said everyone wants "people they can rely on" — and "I think Ford's done the best at it. And especially with their service business, I think they're doing a great job. It's an iconic brand that's also evolving and moving forward."

Bargatze said he likes that the company is making the servicing of cars "simple for you, and they use all real Ford parts. ... The pros are trained by Ford." 

NATE BARGATZE TAKES CLEAN COMEDY TO BIG SCREEN WITH ‘THE BREADWINNER’ 

He said his Ford Bronco "gets fixed a lot easier when they come to your house."

The campaign is leaning into his relatable humor to make vehicle service feel less intimidating, the Dearborn, Michigan-based company said — while highlighting its parts, factory-trained technicians and convenient-to-consumer service options.

For the average American today, Bargatze said that "everything is so polarizing, and everything is so extreme and life or death. But you know — not that [certain] things aren't serious — but [a lot of life] is people just taking their kids to school, and they've got to drop off three kids, and then you've got a soccer game and a baseball game. And, you know, you're just living life."

He said things in today's world have been "sped up, and it's been speeding up more and more. So I think people want to take a breath, they want to take a step back. Not everything needs to be so polarizing. Things can still be just simpler, and I've seen that with the tour that I go on."

‘SHUT UP AND LISTEN’ — TRACE GALLAGHER SHARES ‘UNEXPECTED’ WISDOM LEARNED FROM BEING A ‘GIRL DAD’ 

He does not include politics in his stand-up routines. 

"You know, it's a ton of people [just] coming out, and they get to have fun, and they get to laugh ... and I want to be there for them."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES

He said he believes his comedy shows are a time for people to "take a break, and it's a moment to not worry about the stresses of your life."

That's the parallel he sees with Ford, he said. 

"It fits! Ford has their parts. So when you buy a Ford car, it's not complicated. You have it [all] from one place. The people that are making it — they're coming to help fix your car or take care of your car. It is from Ford. So I think it's a big trust issue."

He added, "It's their values and what they stand for and the trust that they have — that's exactly what I want to do with making movies [and] doing stand-up. I want people to be able to rely on it and know what to expect, and not be surprised by it. And just be trusted."

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

His approach to comedy, he said, is simple and down to earth.

"I make fun of me. I make fun of myself ... and I try not to go outwards."

He said, "When you keep it that simple, that's why it works. No one feels like when they come to the show that it's going to be about them, or that I'm going to be making fun of something that they like or don't like — whatever it is. I'm just talking about me and my family and stuff that we go through, the everyday kind of things."

He added, "I think that's why people can relate to it now. ... And I think stand-up comedy can stand the test of time. It can't get any more authentic than just a person talking to an audience."

The Des Plaines Police Department told OutKick Dropkick there were no indications of foul play and the circumstances around Satterley’s death were not deemed to be suspicious. Police said the cause of death would be determined by the Cook County Medical Examiner’s Office.

AEW announced Satterley’s death late Sunday, sending shock and disbelief across the pro wrestling world.

"All Elite Wrestling is saddened to announce the passing of Benjamin Satterley, aka Pac," the company said. "A native of Newcastle upon Tyne, England, Satterley began his wrestling career in 2004 and went on to perform for wrestling organizations all over the world, captivating fans with innovative high-flying moves and incredible in-ring ability.

"Pac signed with All Elite Wrestling in 2019 and held multiple AEW Championships and competed in some of the most memorable matches in AEW history. Our condolences go out to Satterley’s family, friends and fans."

AEW owner Tony Khan also paid tribute to Satterley in a separate post.

"Benjamin Satterley defined excellence, as a beloved husband & friend to his many loved ones, + in his wrestling knowledge, skill, unprecedented athleticism, professionalism, consistency + dedication to the sport that he loved & traveled the world to pursue," he wrote on X. "May Ben rest in peace."

Satterley was found "passed out" outside of a CAVA restaurant at around 4 p.m. local time, the California Post reported, citing 911 audio. An official who arrived on the scene reportedly said Satterley was dead on arrival.

Satterley, 40, was one of the first wrestlers to sign with All Elite Wrestling in 2019. He was a two-time trios champion and the inaugural all-Atlantic champion.

Before wrestling in AEW, he was with WWE and known as Adrian Neville. Satterley was a two-time cruiserweight champion, an NXT champion and two-time NXT tag team champion.

WWE Chief Content Officer Paul "Triple H" Levesque added to the chorus of tributes.

"Saddened to hear about the death of Ben Satterley known in @WWE as Neville," he wrote on X. "I had the pleasure of working with Ben in the early days of @WWENXT. This moment, from NXT Arrival, marked the beginning of a new era for that brand and the men and women on it … and Ben was a major force behind that. item.title: Sylvester Stallone reveals surprising health struggle behind his famously ripped physique
item.description: Sylvester Stallone revealed he became bulimic while prepping for "Rambo" and reached 2.6% body fat during "Rocky III" in a stunning new interview.
item.content:encoded:
Sylvester Stallone is sharing some health obstacles he has faced while playing physically demanding roles over the decades.

The Academy Award-nominated actor, 80, revealed during an interview with The New York Times that he has suffered from an eating disorder.

While prepping for his role in the 1982 movie "Rambo," Stallone — who has authored a new memoir, titled "The Steps" — said he took pains to appear more "animalistic," drawing inspiration from jaguars and cats.

MEN FACE NEW PRESSURE TO STAY ‘HOT’ AS THEY AGE — AND IT’S NOT JUST ABOUT LIVING LONGER

"Then it became an obsession. Really bad. It got to the point where I became bulimic," he said during the interview.

Bulimia nervosa is an eating disorder marked by episodes of binge eating — consuming a large amount of food while feeling a loss of control — followed by purging behaviors such as vomiting, excessive use of laxatives or diuretics, fasting or excessive exercise, according to the National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH).

"I couldn’t hold anything down. Or I didn’t want to keep it down because I became so obsessed with staying at that point of fitness, literally an obsessive body-worship kind of thing," Stallone shared.

CONTROVERSIAL STREAMER CLAVICULAR EXPLAINS VIRAL 'LOOKSMAXXING' TREND AS GEN Z ADOPTS EXTREME REGIMEN

The actor said that while filming "Rocky III," he reached his lowest body fat of 2.6%. The National Academy of Sports Medicine classifies body fat as "dangerously low" if it falls below 8% for men ages 20–69 and below 14% for women ages 20–69.

Stallone also admitted that he took steroids during some time periods. "You have to," he said. "But you do it in a sensitive way — six weeks on, six weeks off … that also took a terrible toll."

Years of injuries sustained while doing his own stunts — something he described as "very masochistic" — have also taken a toll on Stallone’s body, he said, leading to multiple surgeries on his back, shoulder and neck.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"I’ve abused my body," he said. "Everything is held together with baling wire, but I still want to stay in good shape."

Stallone also revealed that he has dealt with anxiety over the decades, recounting the first incident while watching footage from one of his films when he was 36 years old.

"All of a sudden, I stood up and the hair on my neck went up and I started getting hot and I go, ‘I’m dying, this is it, I’m on my way out,’" he said in the interview.

The actor said the panic attacks happened "again and again and again," often resurfacing before high-profile television appearances. As he aged, Stallone continued to experience anxiety and sometimes felt compelled to leave crowded rooms.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Brian Pollack, a licensed clinical social worker and certified eating disorders specialist at Hilltop Behavioral Health in Summit, New Jersey, said it was "incredibly admirable" for Stallone to share his experience.

"There are so many examples of what can take place in Sylvester Stallone's life that have led him to moments of objectivity and body awareness," Pollack, who has not treated Stallone, told Fox News Digital.

The expert suggested that a desire to maintain his success may have fueled Stallone’s rigid routines, steroid use, intense performance expectations, fear of failure, and the pressures associated with the entertainment industry.

"The idea that a man enhances his appearance to remain consistent with his own public image and internal comfort goes back decades — [Stallone] isn’t the first, and he isn’t the last," Pollack said.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"He has to almost keep himself in this homeostatic state where people expect Sylvestor Stallone to be Rocky, which is his quintessential role," he went on.

"And through his career, one could surmise the need to be able to put all of that together and keep it consistent as he goes through the development and life cycles of maturation, not only in his brain, but also in his body."

Giulia Suro, a licensed clinical psychologist and certified eating disorder expert at Monte Nido in Washington, D.C., added that the Sylvester Stallone revelation was a "game-changer."

"Eating disorders continue to be misconstrued as primarily female illnesses," she told Fox News Digital.

item.title: The NFL has officially become flag football, fans are fuming & MLB makes a baffling call ahead of the playoffs
item.description: The final Monday of September brings NFL officiating outrage after a textbook quarterback hit drew a flag in the Chiefs-Dolphins fourth quarter.
item.content:encoded:
'Nightcaps' is a daily column that catches you up on the biggest sports, news and culture stories you may have missed while pretending to do work at your desk. It runs Monday-Friday on OutKick.com.

Final Monday of September. This is it, folks. We're a few days away from October. First full month of football just about in the books.

And now we have the MLB postseason on deck?! Along with more football? How lucky are we? What a country. Goodness, we are blessed.

Solid weekend of sports, right? The golf world is breathing a sigh of relief today after the fellas avoided a catastrophe yesterday. The college football world was, once again, treated to absolute cinema for about 12 hours on Saturday. I actually thought the NFL had a really nice bounce back Sunday after a lackluster Week 2 ...

Except for the officiating. It completely ruined everything, as it tends to do. It was just bad call after bad call. I was stunned at what I saw in yesterday's Dolphins-Chiefs game. Stunned. Somehow, it got even worse in last night's thriller in Denver.

It's just so, unfathomably bad at this point. And there is no accountability. It's disgusting. We'll dive in here in a bit.

But first, welcome to a Monday Nightcaps — the one where you officially cannot touch, breath, or even look at a quarterback in the National Football League anymore. Sad.

NFL WEEK 3 SUNDAY TAKEAWAYS: PATRIOTS HAVE A MAYE PROBLEM, CHARGERS HIT ROCK BOTTOM AND COWBOYS CRUMBLE

What else? I've got Cam Ward being quite possibly the biggest bust of my lifetime, a ballboy in Jacksonville picking a fight with a massive defensive end over a football, and how about the BS move Major League Baseball pulled this weekend?

Is Manfred serious with this? What a joke. You'll see.

OK, let's get this class — and week — started. It's a Monday night, after all. We've got MORE football to watch.

Grab you a beer for National Drink Beer Day (solid holiday!) and settle in for a Monday 'Cap!

Let's go ahead and jump right in. No beating around the bush on this final Monday of September.

So, the horrible Miami Dolphins lost to the not-horrible Kansas City Chiefs yesterday in a game that was surprisingly close. Credit to Miami for looking markedly better. Credit to the Chiefs for still covering the spread.

Win-win!

Miami actually had a legit shot to win this game, believe it or not. Trailing 17-10 to start the fourth quarter, the Dolphins had the Chiefs backed up into their own end zone on third and long. Patrick Mahomes dropped back to pass, and was absolutely crushed by Chop Robinson, forcing an incomplete pass.

It looked like a textbook quarterback hit, which is nearly impossible to do given the ridiculous rules nowadays. Helmet to the chest, and putting the arms out on the way down to catch himself as to not land on Mahomes with his full body weight.

Again — stupid rules — but Chop appeared to follow them to a tee ...

Key word there being "appeared."

What are we doing here? Seriously. It's just so silly at this point. If that's a penalty, the defenders truly have no chance in this league. None. WHAT is he supposed to have done differently?

And by the way, I'm not saying it was the wrong call. It wasn't. It was the right call.

The RULE itself is mind-numbingly stupid. Here's Rule 12, Section 2, Article 11(b) in the NFL rulebook:

A rushing defender is prohibited from committing such intimidating and punishing acts as "stuffing" a passer into the ground or unnecessarily wrestling or driving him down after the passer has thrown the ball, even if the rusher makes his initial contact with the passer within the one-step limitation provided for in (a) above.

When tackling a passer who is in a defenseless posture (i.e. before, during, or after throwing or attempting a pass), a defensive player must not unnecessarily or violently throw him down or land on top of him with all or most of the defender’s weight. Instead, the defensive player must strive to fall to the side of the passer’s body, or to brace his fall with his arms to avoid landing on the passer with all or most of his body weight.

It's just such a silly rule. "All or most of his body weight." What does that even mean? That's the most subjective rule I've ever seen.

How does a ref determine how much body weight one is falling with? Between this and the ridiculous pass interference call that cost the Rams the game last night, it was just a really poor Sunday for NFL refs.

And I mean REALLY poor:

Just horrible. I said it last year. I said it the year before. I've said it every year for a decade now: NFL officiating is ruining the game. So are the rules.

It's insane. Frankly, it's sad.

OK, let's move it along and check in with last year's first overall pick, Cam Ward!

Speaking of bad NFL Sundays ...

I've never seen a quarterback do that before. Ever. What is that? Cam Ward, by the way, is now 3-17 as a starter. Pretty big sample size at this point.

And he's still acting like THAT? Hey, buddy, why don't you RUN if there's that much time back there and you're bored? Ever think about that? Maybe do a little scrambling and figure something out?

Same with the goal line play at the end. He had the pylon right in front of him. Just keep running! Instead, he just throws a duck to the Giants and it was curtains.

The No. 2 pick behind Ward last year? That would be Travis Hunter.

Speaking of Hunter, let's rapid-fire this Monday class into a big night of FOOTBALL. Congrats on your first career INT, Travis!

Just a weird Sunday in the NFL, right? What's going on here? Why is this guy getting so defensive?

"Hey! Don't touch me! Do not touch me!" he says as he tries to slap 6-foot-5, 255-pound Josh Hines-Allen away. Good luck, pal. You're gonna need it!

Here's the best part ... that wasn't even the weirdest part of that game yesterday! Anyone see what Trevor Lawrence pulled with 8 minutes left?

Couple things here ...

OK, on the way out, let's quickly check in on how Major League Baseball treated the final Sunday of the season for the Red Sox and Yankees ahead of their Wild Card Series this week:

For those who missed it, the Red Sox and Cubs had to fly to Florida to play Game 162 at Tropicana Field yesterday. It was a meaningless game, as both teams had already clinched everything they could clinch.

The Yanks and Orioles, meanwhile, got rained out and MLB told them not to worry about it.

Okeedokee! Makes sense.

Whatever. MLB postseason starts tomorrow. Four games, all day long, beginning at 2 p.m. with Braves-Phils. Can't wait.

Nothing better than some playoff baseball.

Sox in 3.

Now, let's have a week.

item.title: In-laws arrested after New York Times Games engineering director found fatally shot
item.description: Jonathan McKinsey, 40, was pronounced dead at the scene after a shooting Saturday afternoon, and police arrested his parents-in-law on suspicion of murder within minutes.
item.content:encoded:
Jonathan McKinsey, a New York Times Games engineering executive, was shot and killed Saturday afternoon in Dublin, California, and his wife's parents were arrested on suspicion of murder within minutes, authorities said.

McKinsey, 40, was found with multiple gunshot wounds in the parking lot of the Dublin Sports Grounds and was pronounced dead at the scene, according to the City of Dublin.

A New York Times spokesperson confirmed to Fox News Digital that McKinsey served as director of engineering for New York Times Games. He had worked for the company since January 2023.

At about 3:08 p.m. local time Saturday, a Dublin Police Services sergeant driving near the sports complex spotted a man lying in the parking lot and stopped to investigate.

GEORGIA MAN, 18, CHARGED WITH MURDER AFTER DISMEMBERED HUMAN REMAINS FOUND IN CAR TRUNK

Around the same time, dispatchers began receiving multiple 911 calls reporting a shooting, authorities said.

Responding officers found McKinsey suffering from multiple gunshot wounds. With help from witnesses, officers quickly identified and detained two suspects who had remained at the scene, police said.

The suspects were identified as Shouyong Zhang, 77, and Shili Chen, 77, both of Dublin. Officials said the married couple are McKinsey's parents-in-law.

Both were arrested on suspicion of murder and booked into Santa Rita Jail, authorities said.

YEMEN-BORN VAPE SHOP OWNER NEAR OLE MISS FLED COUNTRY AFTER SYNTHETIC DRUG TRAFFICKING INDICTMENT: DOCS

Police said there are no outstanding suspects and no ongoing threat to the public.

Detectives are continuing to investigate the circumstances surrounding the fatal shooting and have not released a possible motive.

"DPS thanks the witnesses and community members who assisted responding officers; their cooperation was critical to the swift arrest of the suspects," officials said.

Zhang and Chen are scheduled to be arraigned Wednesday at 9 a.m. PT in the East County Hall of Justice in Dublin.

Court records obtained by Fox News show McKinsey was involved in several ongoing legal proceedings at the time of his death, including a child abuse case filed in October 2025 charging him with "cruelty to a child by endangering the health and corporal injury to a child." 

Records show that a pretrial hearing in that case was scheduled for Sept. 10.

Separate court records show McKinsey and his wife, Candice Jang, filed domestic violence restraining order requests against one another in 2025.

The records indicate the cases involved custody disputes.

McKinsey also filed for divorce in December 2025, and a status hearing was scheduled for Oct. 10.

Dublin Police Services did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's requests for comment.
